title: W-35: enforce a minimum backup passphrase and warn on a weak one
description: Source: the consolidated pre-public security review (opum-doc, 2026-10-30), reviewed at b1dae53374a8c0c3514f015ff77faac9af643e2d; tracked under ODOC-552 and parent WCLI-95. Report id: W-35, ruling A. Ruling A: enforce a minimum and warn on a weak one. Today only an empty passphrase is refused (src/adapters/passphrase.ts, src/application/backup.ts), so a one-character passphrase protects every secret in every project at roughly 0.1 s per offline guess. The exact minimum or entropy estimate is a design detail to confirm with opum-doc before the build.

acceptanceCriteria.text: A passphrase below the minimum is refused with a safe error and a weak one draws a warning
The minimum and the warning wording are recorded, with tests in both directions
The backup command's documentation states that strength is the passphrase's

implementationNotes: DESIGN RULING, opum-doc, 2026-10-30T15:57:41Z, recorded on ODOC-552, relayed by team-lead. Verbatim: "measure in Unicode code points after NFC normalisation. REFUSE below 12. WARN, without refusing, from 12 to 15. No entropy estimator and no dictionary: the spec rightly denies that length is strength, and the floor only stops the trivially weak. The refusal text: "A backup passphrase needs at least 12 characters. It is the only thing protecting every secret in this backup if the file is ever copied." The warning text: "This passphrase is short. If the backup file is ever copied, this passphrase alone protects every secret in it. Four or more random words is a good choice." The 1024-byte bound refuses rather than truncates (W-2/WCLI-97). Test both ways: 11 is refused, 12 warns, 16 is silent." This settles the open minimum noted in the task description; the build is briefed separately after its floor check.
